Summarise groups in a GPU table

Source: R/summarise.R
summarise.tbl_gpu.Rd

Computes aggregations on groups defined by group_by(). Operations are performed entirely on the GPU for maximum performance.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
summarise(.data, ..., .groups = NULL, .by = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
summarize(.data, ..., .groups = NULL, .by = NULL)

Arguments

.data

A grouped tbl_gpu object created by group_by().

...

Name-value pairs of summary functions. The name will be the name of the variable in the result. The value must be a single aggregation expression in the form fun(column), where column can also be any expression the internal expression IR understands (see "Aggregation sub-expressions" below).

.groups

Controls grouping structure of the result (Phase 6, task 3; matches dplyr::summarise()'s own contract exactly, verified empirically against dplyr 1.2.1). One of:

  • NULL (default) – "drop_last" (see below), PLUS an informational message when the result is still grouped (see "The regroup message" below).

  • "drop_last" – drop the LAST grouping variable, keeping the rest (e.g. group_by(a, b, c) -> result grouped by a, b); with only one grouping variable, the result is ungrouped. Same as the default, minus the message.

  • "drop" – the result is always ungrouped.

  • "keep" – every original grouping variable is retained.

  • "rowwise" – the summary runs on the GPU keeping every grouping variable, and the result is a rowwise tbl_gpu by those variables (dplyr::rowwise()); collect() returns dplyr's own rowwise_df.

On a rowwise tbl_gpu (see rowwise.tbl_gpu()) summarise() computes one row per input row, the rowwise variables first. .groups = NULL (and "keep") groups the result by those variables (with dplyr's message when .groups is not given), "drop" ungroups it, "rowwise" keeps it rowwise; "drop_last" is an error, as in dplyr. .groups= is only validated against an already-grouped .data – matching a genuine (if surprising) dplyr quirk verified empirically: any value other than "rowwise" (including a typo) is silently a no-op on an UNGROUPED .data, since there is nothing to drop/keep/peel from an empty group set.

The regroup message

When .groups is left NULL (the default) and the pre-summarise .data has MORE THAN ONE grouping variable, an informational message is emitted (loosely matching dplyr's own wording – this is informational, not a value under parity test). It is suppressed by options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE) (an explicit TRUE/FALSE value for this option always wins outright); with the option unset, dplyr's own rule applies: the message only fires when the CALLING code's top environment is the global environment (i.e. top-level/ interactive use) – it is silent when summarise() is called from inside a function/package (as in a testthat test, or one verb calling another, e.g. tally.tbl_gpu()).

.by

Optional on-the-fly grouping columns (tidyselect), GPU-native (Phase 5, task W9). Unlike mutate()/filter()'s .by= (which behave exactly like group_by()), summarise(.by=) has one genuinely different rule verified empirically against dplyr 1.2.1: groups are emitted in FIRST-APPEARANCE order (the order each distinct .by combination first appears in .data), not sorted group-key order – see ".by group order" below. The result is always ungrouped – unlike a group_by()-driven summarise(), whose result's grouping now depends on .groups= (Phase 6, task 3); .groups= can't be combined with .by= at all (rejected by dplyr's own summarise() generic). Supplying .by when .data is already grouped (via group_by()) is an error, matching dplyr exactly.

Value

A tbl_gpu object with one row per group containing the grouping columns and computed aggregations.

Details

Supported aggregation functions

  • sum(x) - Sum of values. Over an integer or logical x the result is an integer, as in dplyr; if it leaves R's integer range (+-(2^31 - 1)) dplyr returns a double, and so does tbl_gpu. Which one it is depends on the data, which a lazy plan (its schema is fixed before it runs) can't know, so a lazy summarise() of an integer (INT32) sum(x) runs at the verb, like an eager one: the pending steps run first (a plan break, see cuplyr.plan_break) and the result is a lazy table with nothing pending. The same goes for a lazy min()/max() of an integer. A sum() of a logical x stays in the plan: it can only overflow with more than 2^31 TRUE rows in a group, and then raises a cuplyr_error_sum_overflow error at collect().

  • mean(x) - Arithmetic mean

  • min(x) - Minimum value

  • max(x) - Maximum value

  • n() - Count of rows in each group

  • sd(x) - Standard deviation

  • var(x) - Variance

  • median(x) - Median value (Phase 6, task 6.2)

  • quantile(x, probs) - A single quantile, probs a scalar in [0, 1] (Phase 6, task 6.2; only one probability per call is supported)

  • n_distinct(x) - Count of distinct values, NA counted as its own distinct value by default (Phase 6, task 6.2)

  • first(x) / last(x) / nth(x, n) - The first/last/nth value in the group's current row order (Phase 6, task 6.2)

  • any(x) / all(x) - Logical reductions with R's own three-valued logic (Phase 6, task 6.2; x must be logical)

Aggregation sub-expressions

column is not limited to a bare column name: any expression the same expression IR that powers filter.tbl_gpu()/mutate.tbl_gpu() understands is computed as a hidden temporary column first, then aggregated. This covers comparisons and logic (sum(carb > 3 & wt < 4), any(carb > 3)), arithmetic (mean(hp / wt)), and math functions (mean(sqrt(hp)), sum(carb %% 2 == 0)), arbitrarily nested – the same surface documented in mutate.tbl_gpu. A comparison/logical sub-expression is summed as TRUE/FALSE -> 1/0, matching R's own coercion (sum(c(TRUE, TRUE)) is 2L) – except inside any()/all(), which keep it logical. An expression shape the IR doesn't recognize raises the same "Invalid aggregation expression" error as any other unsupported aggregation shape.

column may also be (or contain) a WINDOW-function call (Phase 6, task 4), e.g. last(cumsum(v)), sum(v - lag(v, default = 0)), mean(cumsum(v) - lag(cumsum(v))): the window function is computed PER GROUP first (over each group's own row order, using the same window-decomposition engine mutate.tbl_gpu() uses), and the aggregation then reduces that per-row window result – matching dplyr's own two-step semantics exactly. Only ONE aggregation's own argument tree is decomposed this way: combining TWO SEPARATE aggregation calls at the dot level (sum(cumsum(x)) - mean(y)) is not supported (the same "Invalid aggregation expression" error as any other dot that isn't a bare fn(single_arg) shape).

NA handling

mean()/sum()/min()/max()/sd()/var()/median() all match R's own na.rm = FALSE default (Phase 6, tasks 6.1/6.2): if a group contains ANY NA in the aggregated column, the WHOLE group's result is NA for that aggregation – e.g. summarise(m = mean(x)) is NA for a group with even one NA value of x, matching real dplyr exactly. Pass na.rm = TRUE explicitly (e.g. sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)) to exclude NA values instead (cudf's own native aggregation behavior). n() is unaffected by na.rm= (it counts every row regardless of nulls, like dplyr's own n()).

When na.rm = TRUE and a group's aggregated column is ENTIRELY NA (Phase 6, task 4), the result matches base R's own empty-vector reduction identity, exactly like real dplyr: sum() -> 0, mean() -> NaN, min() -> Inf, max() -> -Inf (with base R's warning "no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf" / "... max; returning -Inf", as dplyr surfaces it, for double and integer input alike; it is only raised when some group actually hits the identity), sd()/var()/ median() -> NA (their natural result already, no special-casing needed).

Over an INTEGER column, dplyr promotes the WHOLE min()/max() result column to double the instant any group needs the identity, and keeps it integer otherwise; cuplyr does the same. Because that type depends on the data, a summarise() with an integer min()/max() runs immediately even on a lazy table (pending operations are computed first), and the result's schema reflects the real type. A 0-row input also counts as an empty group: ungrouped, summarise() returns one row of empty-vector reductions (n() 0, mean() NaN, sum() 0, min() Inf, ...); grouped, the result has no rows but an integer min()/max() is typed double, as in dplyr.

quantile() diverges from the mean/sum/.../median family: matching base R's own quantile.default() exactly, na.rm = FALSE (the default) with an actual NA present is a hard ERROR ("missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE"), not a NA result – pass na.rm = TRUE to compute the quantile over the non-NA values instead.

n_distinct() counts NA as its own distinct value when na.rm = FALSE (the default, matching dplyr's own n_distinct() exactly) – e.g. n_distinct(c(1, 2, NA, 2)) is 3. Pass na.rm = TRUE to exclude NA from the distinct count instead.

first()/last()/nth() use dplyr's own na_rm= spelling (underscore, not na.rm): na_rm = FALSE (the default) never skips a NA when picking the first/last/nth value (so the result can itself be NA); na_rm = TRUE skips NA values, returning the first/last/nth non-NA value in the group (or NA if the group has none).

any()/all() implement R's exact three-valued logic: any(x) is TRUE if any element is TRUE (regardless of NAs present), NA if there's no TRUE but at least one NA (with na.rm = FALSE, the default), else FALSE; all(x) is FALSE if any element is FALSE (regardless of NAs present), NA if there's no FALSE but at least one NA (with na.rm = FALSE), else TRUE. na.rm = TRUE drops NA values first, matching base R's any()/all() exactly (an all-NA group with na.rm = TRUE is FALSE for any(), TRUE for all(), the empty-vector identity in both cases).

Ungrouped summarise

If .data is not grouped, summarise will compute aggregations over all rows, returning a single-row table.

No expressions

summarise(.data) with no expressions follows dplyr: ungrouped, it returns a one-row table with no columns; grouped, it returns the distinct group keys (one row per group, in group_by()'s ascending, NA-last order) and peels one grouping layer per .groups; with .by, it returns the distinct .by combinations in first-appearance order.

Tables with no columns

cudf cannot hold rows without columns, so a zero-column tbl_gpu keeps its row count on the R side. What that covers: tbl_gpu(), dim(), collect()/as_tibble(), compute()/collapse(), group_by()/ungroup(), zero-dot summarise() (1 x 0), summarise() with dots (a CPU fallback, so n() counts correctly), ungrouped slice()/slice_head()/slice_tail(), bind_rows()/bind_cols() of zero-column tables only, a literal-mask filter(), dplyr_row_slice(), and adding a column with $<-/[[<-. Every other verb, joins with a zero-column side, vctrs operations (vec_size(), vec_slice(), ...), and binding a zero-column table that has rows to one with columns raise an error instead of returning a wrong row count (full support is F14).

Redefining columns

An expression named like a grouping column replaces that key in place (same position, the expression's type; the table stays grouped by that name). An expression that mentions a name an earlier expression created (or a name created twice) sees the new value, as in dplyr; such calls run through the CPU fallback.

Group order

group_by(g) |> summarise(...) returns groups in dplyr's group_by() order: ascending, NA last, strings in the C locale, FALSE < TRUE, factors in level order (gpu_summarise() sorts the small aggregated result by the keys). count()/tally() inherit it.

.drop = FALSE

On a group_by(.drop = FALSE) grouping with a factor key, or on a table whose group keys are fixed (a .drop = FALSE table after filter(), semi_join(), slice(), ..., or a .preserve = TRUE slice), every group of group_data() gets a row, empty ones included, holding each expression evaluated on an empty vector (n() 0, sum() 0, mean() NaN, min() Inf with base R's warning, ...); with no expressions the result is the keys of every group. Such a call materializes a lazy table on the GPU (the row count is data-dependent). The result is regrouped with the input's .drop. Three shapes differ from dplyr or leave the GPU: min()/max() of a Date or POSIXct column is NA for an empty group (dplyr's Inf/-Inf cannot be held by a GPU timestamp column; an uploaded non-finite Date or POSIXct is NA as well, with the warning described in tbl_gpu()), mean() of a Date or POSIXct column is NA for an empty group where dplyr gives a NaN Date/POSIXct, and min()/max() of a character column runs the whole call on the CPU when a group is empty.

.by group order

Verified empirically against dplyr 1.2.1: summarise(.by=) emits one row per distinct .by combination in the order that combination FIRST appears in .data – e.g. summarise(tibble(g = c("b","a","b")), n = n(), .by = g) returns g in the order c("b", "a"), not c("a", "b"). This differs from group_by(g) |> summarise(...), whose groups are sorted. Implemented via a desugar (summarise_by_desugar()): an ungrouped row_number() marks each row's original position, a grouped summarise computes the user's aggregations plus min() of that position per group, and the result is sorted by that minimum (each group's first-appearance position) before the helper column is dropped.

See also

group_by.tbl_gpu for grouping data, collect.tbl_gpu for retrieving results

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  gpu_mtcars <- tbl_gpu(mtcars)

  # Simple aggregation over all rows
  total <- gpu_mtcars |>
    summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg)) |>
    collect()

  # Grouped aggregation
  by_cyl <- gpu_mtcars |>
    group_by(cyl) |>
    summarise(
      avg_mpg = mean(mpg),
      max_hp = max(hp),
      count = n()
    ) |>
    collect()

  # Multiple grouping columns
  by_cyl_gear <- gpu_mtcars |>
    group_by(cyl, gear) |>
    summarise(
      mean_mpg = mean(mpg),
      min_wt = min(wt)
    ) |>
    collect()
}
#> `summarise()` has regrouped the output by dropping the last grouping variable.
#> Summaries were computed grouped by cyl, gear.
#> Output is grouped by cyl.
#> Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message, or `.groups = "keep"`/`"drop"` to retain/drop every grouping level.
